name: Sunnylands
overview: Estate museum and retreat on 200 acres at 37977 Bob Hope Drive in Rancho Mirage, California, the winter home of Walter and Leonore Annenberg (sunnylands.org).

Walter and Leonore Annenberg built it. It welcomed its first guests in March 1966, and Sunnylands Center & Gardens and the renovated estate opened to the public on 1 March 2012 (sunnylands.org). The pages read do not say how the name arose, and no earlier name was found.
In the 1960s the Annenbergs hired architect A. Quincy Jones and interior designer William Haines to create a midcentury modern estate. The house covers 25,000 square feet (sunnylands.org).
funding_verdict: Sunnylands: self-funded: an endowed family trust that does no fundraising
wider_context: English Wikipedia reports that in 1966 the Inquirer, then owned by Annenberg, asked Democratic candidate Milton Shapp whether he had been a mental hospital patient, and Shapp and others blamed the paper for his loss. Annenberg sold the Inquirer and the Daily News to Knight Newspapers in 1969 for $55 million after the controversy.
The same page says Walter was affected by tax evasion charges and other scandals involving his father in the 1930s.
Walter Annenberg, who owned the Inquirer and Triangle, built Sunnylands, and his descendants govern the trust that runs it.

name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens
aliases: Henry E. Huntington Library and Art Gallery
overview: A research library, art museum and botanical garden on the former estate of Henry Edwards Huntington in San Marino, California (Encyclopedia.com).
Founded by Henry Edwards Huntington (1850 to 1927) and his second wife Arabella Duval Huntington (1850 to 1924); set up as a trust in 1919 and opened to the public in 1928 (Encyclopedia.com).

The library holds the Ellesmere manuscript of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (c. 1410), a Gutenberg Bible (c. 1455) and one of two known 1603 editions of Hamlet; the art collection holds eighteenth-century English, American and French paintings, among them Gainsborough's The Blue Boy (c. 1770) (Encyclopedia.com).
funding_verdict: The Huntington: private trust, paid by gifts, endowment income and admissions

name: Hagley Museum and Library
overview: A museum and library on 235 acres along the Brandywine in Wilmington, Delaware, at 200 Hagley Creek Road, with the library at 298 Buck Road (museum website).

The site is where E. I. du Pont founded a gunpowder works in 1802; it includes restored mills, a workers' community and the ancestral home and gardens of the du Pont family (museum website, About Us).

What is there: hundreds of stone ruins of the black powder industry and dozens of restored buildings (museum website). The museum describes the site as the original black powder works of the DuPont Company; the pages read gave no count of museum objects.
funding_verdict: Hagley Museum and Library: private, from donations and investments, on the site of the du Pont family's first works

name: Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library
aliases: Henry Francis du Pont Winterthur Museum
overview: A museum, garden and library at 5105 Kennett Pike, Winterthur, Delaware, in the du Pont family estate (museum website).

Three generations of the du Pont family gardened at Winterthur from 1839, Henry Francis du Pont turned his home into a museum in 1951 and kept the garden until his death in 1969 (museum website, History of the Garden).

What is there: the museum describes its mansion as holding the most significant collection of American decorative arts in the world and says it has more than 90,000 objects, with about 19,000 ceramics; du Pont began collecting in the 1920s and the objects include American glass, textiles, Shaker furniture and colonial metalwork (museum website). The 60 acre garden sits within nearly 1,000 acres of meadows, farmland and waterways (museum website).
funding_verdict: Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library: private, from a founder's gift and endowment, with gifts and admissions

name: Espacio de Arte Contemporáneo (EAC)
overview: Public contemporary art space at Arenal Grande 1930, Montevideo, in the former Miguelete prison (Cárcel de Miguelete); Wikipedia calls it the only national public institution devoted solely to contemporary art.
Opened in July 2010 from a project begun in 2008 by Uruguay's National Directorate of Culture (Dirección Nacional de Cultura) (Wikipedia).

The prison was built in the late 19th century by the architect Juan Alberto Capurro on Jeremy Bentham's panopticon model, with a central watchtower and four radial three-storey wings, and held prisoners for over a century until it closed in the 1990s (Wikipedia). It is a national historic monument (Artefacto, 2021).
funding_verdict: Espacio de Arte Contemporáneo: public: Uruguay's Ministry of Education and Culture

name: Artspace Sydney
overview: Independent, not-for-profit contemporary art space at The Gunnery, 43 to 51 Cowper Wharf Roadway, Woolloomooloo (Artspace site).

Established in 1983 as an artist-run gallery for emerging and early-career artists, in its original home at 11 Randle Street, Surry Hills, a hat factory built in 1912 (Wikipedia). It moved to The Gunnery in 1992 (Artspace site, Wikipedia).

Building: erected around 1900 as a bulk store for the Sydney Morning Herald, used by the Commonwealth for defence until 1948 and squatted by artists in the 1970s and early 1980s. In 1989 the NSW Government proposed selling it. Artists challenged the sale in the Land & Environment Court, and in 1991 the government proposed a visual arts centre there (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Artspace Sydney: government-supported with a benefactor programme: Create NSW and Creative Australia, plus private benefactors
wider_context: In February 2014 the Sydney academic Matt Kiem began a call to boycott the 19th Biennale of Sydney with an open letter of 4 February; 28 of the 90 participating artists then wrote to the Biennale board asking it to end its sponsorship arrangement with Transfield, and the board replied that it would not sever ties (Hyperallergic, Jillian Steinhauer, 21 February 2014).

Transfield Services held a contract worth AUD 1.2 billion to provide and administer offshore detention facilities on Nauru and Manus Island (Apollo, Tim Walsh, 14 March 2014). Luca Belgiorno-Nettis, executive director of Transfield Holdings, resigned as chairman of the Biennale, and the organisers said they would sever ties with Transfield (Apollo, Maggie Gray, 8 March 2014).
Walsh's Apollo article describes the debate over arts sponsorship in Australia as "riddled with difficult questions and double standards".
Artspace was one of the venues of the 2014 Biennale (Apollo, Walsh). The campaign was aimed at the Biennale and its sponsor.

name: HALLE FÜR KUNST Steiermark
overview: Exhibition house for contemporary art in the Stadtpark at Burgring 2, Graz, operated by the Kunstverein Medienturm (association register number 542738445) (website imprint).
Formerly the Künstlerhaus Graz: art associations collected for a building fund from 1903, the fund was confiscated after the 1938 Anschluss, and the house opened on 20 June 1952 (German Wikipedia).

Building: an early-1950s modernist pavilion that the house calls one of the first white cubes in Austria, renovated in 2010 to 2012 by the Graz architect Alfred Bramberger with the Federal Monuments Office and adapted again from 2020 (website, German Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: HALLE FÜR KUNST Steiermark: public: Land Steiermark, the Austrian federal government and the City of Graz
wider_context: In 2018 the Vereinigung Bildender Künstler Steiermark, the Sezession Graz and the Berufsvereinigung Bildender Künstler protested that their exhibition time in the house had been cut from half a year to 2.5 weeks for all associations together, and submitted 66 white canvases to a call for entries Droschl had issued (ORF Steiermark, December 2018).

profil (Stefan Grissemann and Wolfgang Paterno, 22 March 2025) reported cuts to Styrian culture funding under the new FPÖ-led Land government: Edith Draxl, removed as chair of the culture advisory board, gave about 2.5 million euros of annual and project grants in 2024 against 1.4 million euros in 2025, with cuts of 12 to 70 percent or refusals.

In the same piece Kornhäusl said the culture budget rose from just over 60 million euros in 2019 to almost 81 million, most of it for the large institutions. The article does not name the Halle für Kunst; the Land is its owner and main funder.

name: TBA21 (Thyssen-Bornemisza Art Contemporary)
overview: TBA21 is a foundation for art and ecology with its headquarters at Amor de Dios 1 in Madrid, an office at Schottenring 16 in Vienna, TBA21-Academy at Ocean Space in the Chiesa di San Lorenzo in Venice and the Alligator Head Foundation in Port Antonio, Jamaica (TBA21 contact page).

Francesca Thyssen-Bornemisza entrusted TBA21-Academy with bringing the church of San Lorenzo back to life; Ocean Space opened to the public in 2019 (TBA21 website). The Art Newspaper (12 October 2020) says it reopened in March 2019 after a two-year restoration and that Markus Reymann co-founded the Academy with Francesca von Habsburg.

What is there: the site describes 'two decades of art committed to ecology and social justice' and links to a collection catalogue; no object count is given. Programmes in late 2026 include TBA21-Academy's 'The Current V: Ancestral Ocean', an exhibition by Seba Calfuqueo at the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid (6 October 2026 to 17 January 2027) and Ocean STAGE in Busan (17 September 2026 to 14 March 2027) (TBA21 website).
funding_verdict: TBA21: private, a collector's foundation; no donor or budget figures on the pages read

name: Bahrain National Museum
overview: Bahrain's national museum, on an artificial peninsula facing Muharraq, next to the Bahrain National Theatre (Bahrain Confidential, 14 May 2026).
The late Amir Shaikh Isa bin Salman Al-Khalifa inaugurated it in December 1988 (The Daily Tribune, 26 October 2025).

Six main halls: Burial Mounds, with burial models and grave goods from mounds of about 2250 to 1700 BCE, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019; Dilmun, with seals and pottery; Tylos and Islam, with glassware, jewellery, Umayyad coins and gravestones from the Khamis Mosque; Customs and Traditions; Traditional Crafts, with a life-size model of a souq; and Documents and Manuscripts, with Qurans and papers of the Al Khalifa family (Bahrain Confidential, 14 May 2026). The pages read gave no count of objects.
funding_verdict: Bahrain National Museum: public, under the Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities; no budget stated

name: Netwerk Aalst
overview: Contemporary art and film centre at Houtkaai 15, 9300 Aalst, on the right bank. It calls itself an open house for contemporary art and film (NW website).

Founded in 1981 as the socio-cultural centre Netwerk in a vacant wholesale building in central Aalst. It moved after 2001 into the former Passementerie Van den Brulle textile factory (Dutch Wikipedia).
The Flemish Community recognised Netwerk Galerij as a visual arts centre and Netwerk as a performing arts centre in 2001, and the merged centre as a visual arts kunsthal in 2005 (Dutch Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: NW: public recognition plus philanthropic and ticket income
